To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) urate transport into rat renal brush border vesicles is an OH(-)-gradient-dependent process; 2) urate-anion exchangers are located on the luminal membranes of proximal tubules; and 3) E3040 is an uricosuric agent that inhibits urate-anion exchanges at the luminal membranes in the proximal tubules of the rat kidney.
E3040, a new anti-inflammatory agent, is a competitive inhibitor of urate uptake into rat renal brush border vesicles.

E3040, a uricosuric drug used for treating hyperuricemia in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, inhibits urate reabsorptive transport by competitively blocking the OH(-) dependent urate uptake into renal brush border membrane.

E3040 is a uricosuric agent that acts on urate transport by inhibiting the OH(-)gradient-dependent uptake of uric acid into the brush border membrane vesicle of rat kidney cortex.
E3040 is a uricosuric drug, and its uricosuric effect is due to the inhibition of urate-anion exchanger at the luminal side of the proximal tubules.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
E3040 acts on urate transport by inhibiting uric acid-anion exchange at luminal membrane of the renal proximal tubules.
E3040 is a uricosuric agent with a weak potency, but it has a potential as a therapeutic agent in the treatment of hyperuricemia.
E3040 and benzbromarone, which have a similar chemical structure, inhibit urate reabsorbtion in the renal tubular cells through the competitive inhibition of OH(-) gradient dependent urate uptake.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the urate reabsorbing mechanism in rat renal tubules is not a carrier-mediated process but a simple diffusion process, and E3040 and benzbromarone inhibit this process by different modes of action.
E3040 and two of its metabolites, E3040 sulfate and E3040 glucuronid, have a uricosuric effect and may be useful in the treatment of hyperuricemia and gout.
